\captionof{figure}{\textbf{Stopping a model does not stop its effects.} \textbf{(a)} Real broker and sink processes. A synthetic agent whose calls are all authorized when issued emits 2 calls/s to 32 concurrent tool calls of 5\,s mean latency (the stable cell with the longest latency, by a fixed rule); stop enforced at once; 3 replicates. The fence's zero is by design; it admits none after enforcement in any of its 84 trials, 12 with the sink killed or late completions. \textbf{(b)} The same cell, median and range at each delay \(L\) from decision to enforcement. Solid marks: the plan's halting prediction \(\lambda(L+w)\), \(\lambda\) measured (1.8/s); observed/predicted 1.25 (median; 0.87--8.24; 36 stable trials). Dotted: \(\lambda L\), a post hoc reading. Halting and revoking differ only by the calls emitted but not yet admitted when the stop lands (median 4 at \(L = 0\), just after a burst of 4 calls; 0--3 otherwise); we did not vary where it lands. \textbf{(c)} Probes on single-node instances (40 runs, 20 races per mechanism). Columns: \emph{surface}, the surface refuses a writer that omits the fence; \emph{forgery}, a writer claiming the new epoch is refused; \emph{races}, no stale write commits after the fence while protocol-following writers run. Filled: every run; open: none; half: some; ring with dot: a trigger we installed; dash: not measurable. Only etcd's RBAC revoke has all three (per-race failure below 14\%, one-sided 95\%, if races are independent); if every writer is trusted to follow the protocol, 4 of 9 held in every race. }\label{fig:v6hero}
\end{minipage}\end{center}
